title: Sum of Array Elements
explanation: The loop condition `i < n - 1` stops one element early, so the last array element (50) never gets added to the sum.

title: Equality Check
explanation: A single `=` assigns b to a instead of comparing them. The assignment expression evaluates to 10 (truthy), so the if-branch always runs � and as a side effect, a now silently holds the value 10.

title: Reverse a String
explanation: Looping all the way to `len` swaps every pair TWICE � once on the way through, once again when the loop reaches the mirrored index � so the string ends up back where it started.

title: Find the Maximum
explanation: Starting `max` at 0 only works if the array actually contains something bigger than 0. Here every element is negative, so nothing ever beats 0 and the wrong "maximum" is printed.

title: Recursive Factorial
explanation: The base case returns 0 instead of 1. Since every level multiplies by the result of the level below it, that single wrong base case collapses the entire product to 0.

title: Even or Odd
explanation: The condition itself is correct, but the two print statements were swapped � so an even number prints "Odd" and an odd number prints "Even".

title: Multiplication Table
explanation: The loop condition `i < 10` stops after i = 9, so the table only prints 9 lines and the "5 x 10 = 50" line is missing.

title: Count Vowels
explanation: "a" (double quotes) is a string literal � a pointer � while 'a' (single quotes) is a char. Comparing a char to a string literal compares a small number to a memory address, which is never true, so the vowel count stays 0.

title: Swap Two Numbers
explanation: C passes arguments by value, so `swap` receives copies of a and b. It swaps its own local copies, but main's original a and b never change.

title: Bubble Sort
explanation: The swap condition uses `<` instead of `>`, so larger elements get pushed to the front instead of the back � the array ends up sorted in descending order, not ascending.

title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
explanation: Without parentheses, `32 * 9.0 / 5.0` is computed first and added to c directly � c itself never gets multiplied by 9/5, so the formula is completely wrong despite looking almost right.

title: Prime Number Check
explanation: The loop starts at i = 1, and every number is divisible by 1. That makes `isPrime` false on the very first check � so no number, not even an actual prime, is ever reported as prime.

title: Palindrome Check
explanation: `len - i` is off by one: when i = 0 this reads `s[len]`, which is the string's null terminator, not its last character. Comparing a real character against '\0' always fails, so even a true palindrome gets rejected.

title: Linear Search
explanation: The two return values are swapped: finding the target returns -1 (normally the "not found" signal), and falling through the loop returns i. The function reports failure when it actually succeeded.

title: Fibonacci (Recursive)
explanation: The second base case returns 2 instead of 1. Since fib(1) feeds into every later term through the recursive sum, that one wrong base case throws off every Fibonacci number from fib(2) onward.

title: Sum of Digits
explanation: `/` and `%` were mixed up. `n / 10` strips off the last digit (used correctly to shrink n), but `n % 10` is what actually extracts the last digit � the sum ends up adding shrinking quotients instead of digits.

title: Leap Year Check
explanation: The century rule is backwards: `year % 100 == 0` should be `!= 0`. A year divisible by 100 is only a leap year if it's also divisible by 400 � 1900 fails that check, but the bug reports it as a leap year anyway.

title: Sum of a 2D Array
explanation: The inner loop bound uses `rows` (2) instead of `cols` (4), so only the first 2 columns of each row get added � the 3rd and 4th columns are silently skipped.

title: Manual String Copy
explanation: The loop copies the characters correctly but never writes a null terminator afterward. `printf` keeps reading past "hello" until it happens to hit a zero byte, printing leftover characters still sitting in the buffer.

title: Reverse Array with Pointers
explanation: A proper swap needs a temporary variable. Here `*start` is overwritten first, so its original value is lost before `*end` can be set to it � the "swap" just duplicates one value into both positions.
